title: Infrastructure: vision stack (robot)
purpose: This is the robot webcam/perception subsystem: it owns the single physical VideoCapture device (CameraManager + camera_utils) and provides an offline intent-based perception pipeline (PersonDetector -> multi-person ByteTracker -> single-user selection -> head pose/gaze estimation -> engagement state machine -> multilingual greeting generation) that decides when the robot should treat a person as an engaged user and greet them. It is a hardware-decoupled, sibling concern to the event-bus-driven services/vision_service.py detection path. Notably, only CameraManager is actually wired into the production robot (via CameraService); the full intent/greeting pipeline is only instantiated by the demo desktop GUI (demo.py).

files.purpose: Subpackage public-API module that re-exports the vision stack's main detector class for importers.
files.notes: Only PersonDetector is re-exported; every other module (CameraManager, IntentPerceptionEngine, ByteTracker, HeadPoseGazeEstimator, GreetingManager, camera_utils) must be imported from its own module.

files.purpose: Thread-safe singleton that guarantees exactly one cv2.VideoCapture in the process, runs a dedicated capture thread distributing the latest frame to subscribers with no buffer buildup, plus an out-of-band async detection thread that produces annotated frames and a person_detected flag.

terms.definition: Design pattern ensuring only one CameraManager/CameraManager._instance exists so the physical webcam device is opened by exactly one VideoCapture handle; constructor raises if instantiated twice.
OpenCV object wrapping a physical camera device; here a single instance is owned by CameraManager and read only inside its capture thread to avoid multi-handle DirectShow contention on Windows.

Latency accumulation caused by an unbuffered camera queue delivering stale frames; CameraManager avoids it by overwriting _latest_frame with each new capture so subscribers only ever see the newest frame.
A callable registered via subscribe() that receives a copy of every freshly captured frame; invoked synchronously on the capture thread, so a slow subscriber can stall acquisition.
The current frame with detection/gaze overlays drawn, produced asynchronously by the detection thread and exposed via get_latest_frame(); set only when a detector is installed.

files.notes: Detection loop only does anything after set_detector() is called; it duck-types an object exposing detect_in_frame(frame) returning res.annotated_frame and res.person_detected (the interface implemented by PersonDetector). No caller in the repo actually calls set_detector(), so the annotation path is effectively dead in production. Capture thread flushes the first 5 frames as sensor warmup (auto-exposure/auto-gain), sleeps ~33ms per loop to hold 30 FPS, and treats 5 consecutive failed reads as a retry-with-backoff event. Subscriber callbacks are invoked synchronously under no lock but iteration copies the subscriber list.

files.purpose: Camera device discovery and initialization helpers: reports OpenCV/platform metadata, scans indices 0..N across DirectShow/CAP_ANY backends, and intelligently opens a camera with resolution/FPS setting, a minimized internal buffer, frame-read retry, and a diagnostics dict.
key_symbols: scan_available_cameras(max_indices=4) -> list of camera metadata dicts
Backend tuples: DirectShow (cv2.CAP_DSHOW) then CAP_ANY on Windows, CAP_ANY otherwise

terms.definition: Windows OpenCV video backend (cv2.CAP_DSHOW) tried first on win32/nt before the generic CAP_ANY backend, because it is more reliable for webcams and exposes the device by index.
OpenCV's automatic backend selector constant; used as the cross-platform fallback when DirectShow is unavailable.
OpenCV property controlling the camera driver's internal frame queue; set to 1 here to eliminate latency buildup from queued stale frames.
Integer device identifier (0, 1, 2, ...) used to open a webcam; open_camera_intelligently tries the requested index then fallback indices [0,1,2].

files.notes: Fallback indices default to [0, 1, 2]; a requested_index >= 90 or < 0 yields a single-candidate list (a sentinel-style path, likely used by mock/headless configurations). On failure returns (None, meta) with meta['status']=='failed' and an error message. Frame-read is retried up to 3 times. Resolution/FPS requested via cap.set() but the actual negotiated values are reported back in meta.

files.purpose: Estimates 3D head pose (pitch/yaw/roll), face distance in meters, and whether the person is looking at the camera, using MediaPipe Face Mesh landmarks solved with cv2.solvePnP and falling back to a geometry-based heuristic from the face-box position when MediaPipe is unavailable.
key_symbols: GazeResult (dataclass: pitch, yaw, roll, distance_m, is_looking, gaze_label)
model_points (6-point 3D generic facial model: nose tip, chin, eye corners, mouth corners)

terms.definition: 3D orientation of the head expressed as pitch (up/down), yaw (left/right), and roll (tilt) angles in degrees, computed from facial landmarks.

OpenCV Perspective-n-Point function that estimates an object's rotation and translation vectors by matching known 3D model points to their 2D image positions; used here to derive the face's rotation matrix.
OpenCV decomposition that extracts Euler angles (pitch/yaw/roll) from a rotation matrix; combined with cv2.Rodrigues to convert the solvePnP rotation vector.
Optional (lazily imported) facial-landmark model mapping a face to 468 landmarks; landmarks 1, 152, 33, 263, 61, 291 are used here as the solvePnP image points.
Approximation used to turn face pixel width into meters: assumes real human face width ~0.15m and focal length equal to image width, giving distance_m = (0.15 * w_img) / face_width.

files.notes: is_looking is a hard threshold: looking iff |pitch|<=20 deg and |yaw|<=20 deg. gaze_label uses emoji strings ('\U0001F441 Looking'/'\U0001F648 Not Looking') which may render incorrectly in non-UTF-8 terminals. The OpenCV fallback (MediaPipe absent) derives yaw/pitch purely from the face box's offset from frame center, scaled to +/-30 and +/-20 degrees — a rough heuristic, not real gaze. Distance math is duplicated (also approximated in intent_engine/tracker callers).

files.purpose: Generates time-aware and randomized multilingual greetings (English, Kannada, Hindi) for the robot with cooldown debouncing and an optional per-session guard that prevents repeat greetings while the same person remains in view.

terms.definition: Preventing the robot from greeting too often by requiring a minimum time (default 7.0s) between any two greetings before a new one may fire.

A latch (_session_greeted) that blocks all further greetings for the lifetime of the current presence session, independent of the cooldown timer; cleared only by reset_session()/reset_cooldown() when the person leaves.
The span of time a single person is in view; while it is active the per-session guard prevents repeated greetings even if tracker IDs recycle.

files.notes: Instantiating default cooldown is 7.0s, matching the value used by IntentPerceptionEngine. Time buckets: morning 5-12, afternoon 12-17, evening 17-22, otherwise generic hello. Greeting copy is college-specific, referencing 'KLE Technological University' and the robot name 'Sparky'. reset_session() clears only the session guard (cooldown timer survives), reset_cooldown() clears both.

files.purpose: The perception state machine that updates multi-person tracking, selects a single primary candidate inside the interaction zone, verifies continuous head-pose/gaze engagement for >=2.0s, fires greeting/engaged/disengaged callbacks, and renders diagnostic overlays on the annotated frame.
key_symbols: RobotPerceptionState (Enum: IDLE, PERSON_DETECTED, TRACKING, VERIFY_INTENT, ATTENTION_CONFIRMED, GREETING, INTERACTION)
IntentResult (dataclass: state, active_person, gaze, annotated_frame, engagement_sec, disengage_sec, greeting_text)
constructor defaults: min_interaction_dist=0.5, max_interaction_dist=2.0, engagement_required_sec=2.0, disengage_timeout_sec=1.0, active_language='en'

terms.definition: A distance band (0.5-2.0m) in front of the robot within which a person is eligible to be the primary user; people outside are ignored as passersby/onlookers.
The discrete robot states (IDLE -> PERSON_DETECTED -> TRACKING -> VERIFY_INTENT -> ATTENTION_CONFIRMED -> GREETING -> INTERACTION) that gate how the robot reacts to camera input.
Continuous evidence that the primary person is attending to the robot: within the interaction zone and gaze.is_looking (pitch/yaw within +/-20 deg) for at least engagement_required_sec (2.0s).
Accumulated seconds the active user has been continuously engaged (or turned away) while the timer is active, used to confirm attention and to reset to IDLE.
Once a primary candidate is chosen, active_track_id pins the interaction to that single track ID for the rest of the session until they leave or disengage.

files.notes: Owns its collaborators directly: GreetingManager(cooldown_seconds=7.0), ByteTracker(max_lost_frames=15, iou_threshold=0.3), HeadPoseGazeEstimator(). Distance is re-approximated here as (0.15 * w_img) / max(10, fw) rather than reusing the gaze estimator's distance. At ATTENTION_CONFIRMED a greeting fires only if GreetingManager's cooldown/per-session guard allows it, then the state advances immediately to INTERACTION and on_user_engaged is called. The docstring describes a 5-stage sequence while the Enum defines 7 states (VERIFY_INTENT and GREETING are the extras). on_greeting_triggered callback is wrapped in try/except; other callbacks are not.

files.purpose: Top-level detection entry point that converts a raw BGR frame into raw detections (Haar frontal-face cascade first, HOG person detector as fallback), feeds them into the IntentPerceptionEngine, and reports person presence/left with hysteresis via callbacks and a tuple-compatible DetectionResult.
key_symbols: DetectionResult (tuple subclass carrying person_detected, annotated_frame, face_center, face_forward while preserving 2-tuple unpacking)
_init_detector() (loads Haar face cascade, Haar eye cascade, HOG default people detector)
constructor params: webcam_index=0, reset_frames_threshold=30, on_person_entered, on_person_left, on_greeting_triggered

terms.definition: OpenCV cascade classifier trained on frontal faces (haarcascade_frontalface_default.xml) used as the primary detector; runs on a 320px-wide downscaled grayscale frame for speed.
OpenCV Histogram-of-Oriented-Gradients people detector (HOGDescriptor_getDefaultPeopleDetector) used as a fallback when no faces are found, detecting whole-body boxes.
Debouncing that requires a sustained run of misses (_missing_counter >= reset_frames_threshold=30 frames) before declaring the person gone, and fires on_person_left only then to avoid flicker.
The frame is resized to a 320px-wide grayscale image before detection, and resulting boxes are scaled back to full resolution, to keep face/person detection ultra-fast on the Pi.

config: settings.person_detection_reset_frames (passed as reset_frames_threshold by demo.py; default 30)
files.notes: Detection confidences are hardcoded (faces 0.95, HOG 0.75). detect_in_frame contains its own person-entered/left hysteresis logic (lines ~185-199) IN ADDITION to the intent-engine callbacks (_handle_user_engaged/_handle_user_disengaged), so on_person_entered/on_person_left can be double-fired. The infra PersonDetector is only instantiated in demo.py (desktop GUI); robot_main.py uses services.vision_service.MockPersonDetector instead, so this full intent/greeting pipeline is not part of the production robot path.

files.purpose: Persistent multi-person tracker that assigns stable integer IDs to detected people across consecutive frames via greedy IoU matching and centroid updates, pruning stale tracks and returning the current frame's active tracks.
key_symbols: TrackedPerson (dataclass: track_id, bbox, centroid, confidence, first_seen, last_seen, lost_count, is_active_user; area property)
ByteTracker (class: update(detections), max_lost_frames=15, iou_threshold=0.3, next_id, tracks dict)

terms.definition: Intersection over Union — the overlap of two bounding boxes divided by their union; used to decide whether a detection matches an existing track.
A stable identity (track_id) attached to one person across frames; matched by highest IoU and updated with the newest bbox, centroid, and confidence.
Frames a track has gone unmatched; tracks are deleted once lost_count exceeds max_lost_frames (15) and only tracks with lost_count==0 are returned as active.
The center pixel (cx, cy) of a detection box, stored on each track and used for distance/position logic by the intent engine.

files.notes: Despite the name, this is NOT the academic BYTETrack algorithm — it is a simplified custom greedy-IoU + centroid tracker with no Kalman filter, velocity prediction, or two-stage low-score association, so track IDs can swap under occlusion or fast motion. Matching is greedy: repeatedly takes the highest-IoU pair above the threshold and zeroes that row/column.

data_flow: CameraService (services/camera_service.py) is the production consumer of the camera half: on initialize() it calls CameraManager.get_instance().start_camera(index, resolution, fps) and its _read_frame() pulls raw frames from CameraManager.get_latest_frame() (deliberately NOT opening a second VideoCapture, to avoid DirectShow contention); system_runtime.py probes CameraManager.is_running() during startup health checks and passes the camera-ok signal into event handling. The perception half (PersonDetector -> IntentPerceptionEngine -> ByteTracker / HeadPoseGazeEstimator / GreetingManager) is instantiated only in demo.py and handed to ModernChatWindow (presentation/chat_window.py) as the desktop GUI detector; its outputs are annotated frames plus callbacks (on_person_entered, on_person_left, on_greeting_triggered) that drive GUI/robot reactions. In robot_main.py the production stack instead wires services/vision_service.py (VisionService + MockPersonDetector/HOGPersonDetector) onto the event bus — a parallel, independent detection implementation. CameraManager.set_detector() exists to attach a PersonDetector-style object to its async detection thread, but no code path calls it. Data passed is always raw BGR numpy frames in and (raw, annotated, diagnostics) tuples / IntentResult / DetectionResult out.
external_deps: OpenCV (cv2): VideoCapture, CascadeClassifier (haarcascade_frontalface_default.xml, haarcascade_eye.xml), HOGDescriptor default people detector, solvePnP/Rodrigues/RQDecomp3x3, cap properties (CAP_DSHOW, CAP_ANY, CAP_PROP_BUFFERSIZE)
numpy (ndarray frames, IoU matrix, model points)
MediaPipe (optional, lazily imported mediapipe.solutions.face_mesh for gaze estimation; skipped gracefully when absent)
risks: Only CameraManager is wired into the production robot; the entire intent/greeting perception pipeline (PersonDetector, IntentPerceptionEngine, tracker, gaze, greetings) is dead code in robot_main.py — it runs only in the demo GUI (demo.py), while a parallel, duplicate detection stack (VisionService + HOGPersonDetector/MockPersonDetector) is used on the event bus.
No code path ever calls CameraManager.set_detector(), so the async detection thread is a no-op in production: _latest_annotated_frame and _person_detected are never populated.

Gaze and distance are heuristics, not metrology: distance assumes a 0.15m face and focal length equal to image width; the OpenCV gaze fallback derives pitch/yaw purely from the face box's offset from frame center; the intent engine re-computes distance with its own copy of the same formula.
PersonDetector.detect_in_frame duplicates the person-entered/left logic on top of the intent-engine callbacks, which can double-fire on_person_entered/on_person_left.
ByteTracker is a simplified custom greedy-IoU tracker (no Kalman prediction), so track IDs can swap under occlusion/fast motion, which can confuse the per-session greeting guard.
GazeResult.gaze_label uses emoji ('Looking'/'Not Looking') and the overlay drawing is fixed-size (e.g. 520x48 badge) — brittle for small frames and non-UTF-8 output sinks.
CameraManager invokes subscriber callbacks synchronously on the capture thread; a slow subscriber stalls frame acquisition and inflates the 30 FPS loop timing.
